## Introduction

Starsim is a framework for modeling the spread of diseases, as compartmental models or among agents via dynamic transmission networks. Starsim supports:

- Writing a disease as its states and the transitions between them (compartments and the rates of flow between them, as in a textbook model), and running the same model as a deterministic compartmental model, as a stochastic one, or as agents
- Co-transmission of multiple diseases at once, capturing how they interact biologically and behaviorally
- Non-infectious diseases, either on their own or as factors affecting the transmission or mortality of infectious diseases
- Detailed modeling of mother-child relationships starting from conception, allowing investigation of infant and childhood diseases
- Multiple types of transmission network, including theoretical (e.g. Erdős–Rényi) and realistic (e.g. age-assortative sexual partnerships)
- Different intervention types, such as vaccines or treatments, and showing their impact through different delivery methods such as mass campaigns or targeted outreach
- Calibration to data, and common random numbers, so that two scenarios differ by what was changed rather than by chance

Starsim is available for both Python and R, and is fully open-source under the MIT license.

## Types of disease modeling

Starsim models can be compartmental or agent-based (an ABM). A disease written as states and transitions can be run either way: as compartments when the model can be written as compartments, and as agents when something in it needs individuals, such as a network of who is in contact with whom. Starsim chooses which, and says so; it can also be told (see [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd)). Parts of a model written as Python code, such as a custom intervention, run as agents. ABMs are most suitable for questions that are moderately complex, and have medium to large amounts of data available:

![Types of model](assets/types_of_model.png)

For simpler questions, statistical or compartmental models are often all that's needed. For very complex questions, machine learning models may be more suitable. Examples of each type of question are:

- **Statistical models**: "Are people who received the vaccine less likely to get infected?"
- **Machine learning models**: "What behavioral factors influence vaccination uptake?"
- **Compartmental models**: "What is disease prevalence going to be in 5 years given 100% vaccine uptake?"
- **Agent-based models**: "What is disease prevalence going to be in 5 years given realistic assumptions about screening and vaccine coverage?"

Because a declared Starsim model can be run both ways, the choice need not be made up front: a model can start as compartments, and be run as agents once a question needs individuals (and the two can be compared, to see what the individual detail changes). The [conceptual overview](intro_concepts.qmd) explains how this works.

## Why Starsim?

Starsim aims to address the limitations of existing ABMs, specifically along the dimensions of usability, capability, and outcome:

| Dimension | Starsim | Status quo |
|----------|----------|----------|
| Usability   | Starsim is fast, has a simple interface, and requires knowledge of Python (or R) only   | Many ABMs are slow, complex, or require knowledge of C++/Java   |
| Capability   | Starsim supports multiple custom diseases and networks, including co-transmission   | Most other disease models are single-disease or hard-coded to a handful of diseases   |
| Outcome   | Once you've collected your data, modeling your questions with Starsim takes days to weeks   | Writing, testing, and calibrating a custom model can take months to years   |

While of course not all existing ABMs have these limitations, many of them have at least one. (For a good review of general-purpose ABMs, see [Antelmi et al. 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/1/13)). For how Starsim relates to other modeling frameworks, see the [modeling landscape](library_landscape.qmd).

## Starsim principles

Starsim's design philosophy has two parts. First, "**Common tasks should be simple**". Examples include:

- Defining parameters
- Running a simulation
- Plotting results

These are things you need to do in every single Starsim analysis, so we've tried to make them as easy as possible.

The second part of the philosophy is "**Custom tasks can't always be simple, but they should still be possible**". Examples include:

- Introducing a new vaccine
- Implementing a new disease
- Writing a custom calibration function

If you're implementing a complicated disease, there will always be some irreducible complexity involved in that. Starsim's job is to help you where it can, but then get out of the way and let you write your code.

## Should I use Starsim?

Starsim is suitable for many use cases, but not all. Some examples of suitable Starsim use cases are:

- If you are currently doing agent-based modeling but your model is too slow/inflexible/hard to use for your research questions
    - *Example*: Your model takes 14 hours for a single run, and every year you're worried that your computing grant won't be renewed
- If you are currently doing compartmental modeling, and want to try out an agent-based model without investing 3-6 months learning how to use it
    - *Example*: Your compartmental mpox model has so far been very effective, but you've been asked to evaluate an individually-targeted intervention that requires tracking individual agents. In Starsim, the same model can be run as an ODE and as agents, and the two compared
- If you want to quickly prototype different diseases or networks before deciding whether to implement them in your full model
    - *Example*: You know and love your HIV model, but you want to see what the impact would be of including syphilis co-transmission or a different type of MSM network

However, there are other cases where Starsim may not be suitable. These include:

- If you are doing a very simple modeling task, such as a simple SIR or SEIR model, you might as well use plain Python or R. Starsim is fast and concise, but is unlikely to be faster or significantly more concise than well-written custom code. But if your script starts getting longer than about 100 lines, and if you want to do calibration or handle different time units, there is a good chance that Starsim would be able to make things easier.
- If your current model is highly specialized to a given context, the switching cost of moving to Starsim may not be worthwhile. Starsim can import models from several other frameworks (see [Import and export](conversion/index.qmd)), and AI tools make translating a model much easier than it used to be, so get in touch if this is of interest to you.

## Finding your way around

These docs are organized by what you want to do:

- **To see Starsim in action**, take the [tour](../tour.qmd), which builds and runs a model in a few minutes, or browse the [gallery](../gallery.qmd) of complete models.
- **To learn Starsim**, follow the [tutorials](../tutorials.qmd) in order. The core tutorials (T1 to T9) build up one measles model, from a simple SIR to age groups, vaccination, geography, calibration, and custom code; the agent-based tutorials (A1 to A5) cover networks, demographics, and modules that need individuals.
- **To look something up**, use this user guide. Each page is a complete reference for one topic, such as [writing models](building_writing.qmd), [time](building_time.qmd), or [running scenarios](running_scenarios.qmd), and links to the tutorial that introduces it. The [Architecture](architecture_index.qmd) pages explain how Starsim works under the hood.
- **For the exact arguments of a function**, see the [API reference](../api/index.qmd).
- **If you are coming from another framework** (Starsim 3, EpiModel, odin, epydemix, and others), see [Conversion](conversion/index.qmd), which has a page for each.

A runnable example is a starting point, not a calibrated model of a particular population: a model's scientific validity depends on its assumptions, the evidence behind its parameters, and the checks made against data.

## Further reading

- [Covasim: An agent-based model of COVID-19 dynamics and interventions](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009149): the paper on Starsim's predecessor, with a discussion of when agent-based models are worth their cost
- [Appropriate models for the management of infectious diseases](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0020174): how a model's structural assumptions (such as exponential durations) change its predictions
- [Epiverse: tools for epidemic analytics](https://epiverse-trace.github.io/): a collection of R packages for outbreak analysis and compartmental modeling
- [EpiModel](https://www.epimodel.org/): an R framework for network models of infectious disease
- [Mesa](https://mesa.readthedocs.io/): a general-purpose agent-based modeling framework in Python
